newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Scalfaro turns to history in unity call.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Scalfaro turns to history in unity call.

text.p: Italian President Oscar Luigi Scalfaro urged schoolchildren on Saturday to learn the lessons of history in another call for unity ahead of a planned "declaration of independence" by the separatist Northern League.

"Young people must learn from history how many have given their lives for Italy, for its unity and freedom," Scalfaro, himself a northerner, wrote in an address marking the new academic year which starts on Monday.

"They were like you are today. They were not born heroes, but they believed in the nation, in individual liberty, in the rights of man and for these same values, which are identical today, they paid everything," Scalfaro said.
He concluded that history must be studied to ensure that the "same errors and same tragedies" were not repeated.
It was Scalfaro's second appeal for unity in the past three days. On Thursday, speaking in Venice, he urged Italians to look to their "common roots which no-one can ever shake."

Umberto Bossi, firebrand leader of the Northern League, plans to proclaim his northern "Republic of Padania" in Venice on September 15 after rallies and speeches during the preceding three days at points along the river Po.
Bossi has said he expects one million supporters to throng the banks of the Po, which dissects the country, forming symbolic human chains along its course.
Bossi has built his party's strength on northern discontent with high taxes and the past corruption and inefficiency of central governments in Rome.

He moved from a federalist to a separatist platform after the League made a strong showing in April's general election, polling almost four million votes in the north, while failing to secure the balance of power in the national parliament.
Many Italian politicians have mocked Bossi's claims, while others plan alternative events on September 15.

Media mogul and former prime minister Silvio Berlusconi, whose short-lived centre-right government was toppled by Bossi in 1994 when the Northern League withdrew its support, blamed the media for blowing matters out of proportion.
"Stop giving so much importance to an event that will change nothing," he was quoted as saying.

Massimo D'Alema, leader of the main Democratic Party of the Left, told a rally on Friday night in the northern city of Modena that Bossi was "committing a dramatic mistake" and doubting that he would get much of a turnout.
"Nothing serious is going to happen on the 15th," he said.
D'Alema said Bossi had his merits but was mistaken in taking the League, which he said had legitimate grievances, down an extremist path instead of trying to enact reforms.
"We are offended by the secessionist campaign and its racist streak," he said. "The history of Italy is made up of city states and principalities, not inexistent entities," he said.
"If the League continues its boorish campaign against history and aimed at breaking up the country, it will find no friends in the PDS but strong opponents," D'Alema warned.
Newspapers quoted Bossi as ruling out any involvement in constitutional reforms, saying it was too late.
"Reforms cannot be carried out. One can only tinker around a little bit. They've been saying this for years. From now until the 15th, all communications with Rome are ended."
